name: Delhi Quartzite Rubble and Ashlar Masonry
traditional_use: Massive retaining walls, foundations, and well shafts in Delhi NCR, Haryana, and Northern Rajasthan baolis (e.g. Agrasen ki Baoli, Rajon ki Baoli).

moisture_behavior.breathability: Very low intrinsic porosity; impervious crystalline rock matrix
moisture_behavior.capillary_suction: Minimal capillary suction through stone matrix
moisture_behavior.drying_rate: Moisture transport occurs almost exclusively through the mortar joint network
moisture_behavior.summary: Because quartzite is nearly impermeable, the mortar joints must perform 100% of the masonry breathing function.

mechanical_characteristics.stiffness: Very high modulus of elasticity and extreme hardness (Mohs hardness 7)
mechanical_characteristics.ductility: Brittle, high shear and compressive strength
mechanical_characteristics.sacrificial_behavior: Historic substrate; joints must accommodate all shear movement
mechanical_characteristics.summary: Requires ductile, yielding mortar joints to prevent stress concentrations at uneven contact points.

thermal_characteristics.summary: Large temperature swings induce significant expansion; joints must flex to relieve thermal strain.

chemical_considerations.soluble_salts_risk: Resistant to chemical attack, but joint mortar can leach salts onto stone surface
chemical_considerations.summary: Stone is chemically durable, but impermeable nature concentrates salt efflorescence directly on joint edges.

heritage_compatibility.iks_alignment: Traditional Delhi ridge quarry stone extensively used in Sultanate and Mughal hydraulic architecture

limitations: Irregular rubble bedding requires flexible, thick-joint lime mortar rather than thin modern grouts.
Non-breathable cement pointing on quartzite traps water entirely behind the retaining wall, building destabilizing hydrostatic pressure.
